The African diaspora refers to the dispersal of African peoples across the globe, most significantly through the forced migration of enslaved Africans to the Americas between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries, and subsequently through voluntary migration. This vast movement of peoples created enduring communities in the Caribbean, North and South America, and beyond, generating new cultural forms, identities, and traditions that blend African heritage with the experiences of their adopted homelands.

The transatlantic slave trade, spanning from the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries, forcibly displaced approximately twelve million Africans to the Americas. The overwhelming majority were enslaved and labored to death in Caribbean and Brazilian sugar plantations. Yet enslaved Africans maintained their cultural traditions—music, language, spiritual practices, and storytelling—which merged with Indigenous and European influences to create distinct diaspora cultures across different regions. The Caribbean became the primary destination for enslaved Africans, resulting in majority-Black societies where African cultural retentions are most pronounced in music, dance, religion, and cuisine.

Diaspora communities developed new languages—Creoles, Gullah, Jamaican Patois—that blended African grammar and vocabulary with European languages, enabling communication across linguistic groups. After abolition, particularly during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, people from the Caribbean and Africa migrated to North America, Britain, and Europe, expanding the diaspora into metropolitan centers and creating new forms of diaspora identity. Cultural practices including Carnival, Junkanoo, Voodoo, and blues music emerged from diaspora communities, synthesizing African rhythms and spiritual worldviews with New World environments. The diaspora concept itself became central to African-American and Black British identity politics and social movements seeking to reclaim African heritage despite displacement and oppression.
